newsitem.title: USA: Asian Americans feel victimized by scandal.
newsitem.headline: Asian Americans feel victimized by scandal.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, Political Correspondent
Asian Americans fear they may be the collective scapegoats of the Senate hearings into campaign fund-raising scandals, which they say have already produced some crude ethnic slurs aimed against them.

Asians and Asian American individuals have held the spotlight in the first four weeks of hearings by the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee, which are examining the flow of illegal foreign money into the U.S. political system in the 1994 and 1996 elections.

It does not help that many of the main characters, including Democratic Party fund-raiser John Huang, Little Rock restaurateur Yah Lin Trie, entrepreneur Johnnie Chung and Thai-American fund-raiser Pauline Kanchanalak have either fled abroad or are refusing to cooperate with investigators.
Their absence invites some reporters and commentators to use terms like "mysterious," "murky" or "enigmatic" to describe them and their motives.

"Such terms, feeding on the image of the inscrutable outsider, reinforce very negative stereotypes of Asians and Asian Americans," said Daphne Kwok, executive director of the Organisation of Chinese Americans.
So far, most of the senators on the committee have been careful not to spread blame beyond the individuals involved to the entire 10 million-strong Asian American community.
Asian American spokespeople are anxious to stress that any wrongdoing, whether by Asian Americans or others, should be investigated and punished.

"Nobody is defending wrongdoing. But if one person does something wrong, that doesn't mean that other people with similar names or faces or ancestry have done anything wrong," said Frank Wu, a law professor at Howard University in Washington, D.C.
Wu and others interviewed were particularly angered by a comment early in the hearings by Kansas Republican Sen. Sam Brownback.
In what was evidently intended as a witty aside on Huang's fund-raising activities for the Democratic Party, Brownback said: "No raise money, no get bonus."
Brownback immediately apologised for the statement, saying he had meant no offence. His spokesman, Bob Murray, said it was an "unfortunate statement, not meant in a racist way."
A press release compiled by the Congressional Asian Pacific American Caucus Institute (CAPACI) added a couple of other quotes from legislators which it found objectionable.
Utah Republican Sen. Robert Bennett said of Trie: "In my opinion, Mr. Trie's activities are classic activities on the part of an Asian who comes out of that culture."
Representative Jack Kingston, a Georgia Republican, said illegal donations were "apparently only the tip of the egg roll."
Kingston's communications director Robyn Ridgley said the comment was "strictly humorous, as Jack often makes humorous remarks. This was not done at Asian Americans' expense."

Bennett's communications director Mary Jane Collipriest said Bennett had owned businesses in Asia and merely wanted to point out to colleagues that "the Asian business culture is very different from the Western business culture."
But Wu said, "Such comments are not the worst form of racism but taken together, they do reflect a broader uneasiness about the presence of large numbers of Asian immigrants in this country."

"There's a growing fear in this country about the rise of the East and the decline of the West. What better focus for such fears than Asian Americans, who are now portrayed as agents of a foreign influence?" Wu said.
CAPACI executive director Francey Lim Youngberg worries that the most lasting effect of the hearings will be to deter Asian Americans from fully participating in U.S. politics.

Earlier this year, the Democratic Party conducted an audit designed to identify any possibly illegal donations which resulted in the contributions of virtually anyone with an Asian sounding name being questioned.
"There could be a chilling effect. The message is being sent that we are guilty by association and that guilt is going to be held against us," said Youngberg.

"We are a very young community and we are still learning. If people feel they are not welcome or their money is not welcome, they will be deterred from participating in the political process," she said.
